title: Interview Problems
description: Practice common data structure interview problems and learn the patterns that unlock fast, confident solutions.

data.text: Interviews test your ability to map a problem to a data structure and then implement a clean solution. This lesson covers four classic problem patterns, explains the intuition behind each, and walks through worked solutions so you can recognize the pattern in future questions.
Two pointers move through an array or list from different ends or speeds. The technique is useful when the input is sorted or when you want to reduce a nested loop to a single pass.

data.title: Two pointers: check if a string is a palindrome
data.content: Compare characters from the left and right ends while moving inward.

data.text: A sliding window tracks a subset of an array as it moves forward. The technique shines when you need to compute something over every contiguous subarray of a given size or find the smallest window that satisfies a condition.

data.title: Sliding window: maximum sum of size k
data.content: Find the maximum sum of any contiguous subarray of length k.

data.text: Breadth-first search explores neighbors layer by layer. It is the standard tool for shortest-path questions in unweighted graphs and for finding the minimum number of steps to reach a target.

data.title: BFS: shortest path in an unweighted graph
data.content: Return the minimum number of edges from start to target.

data.text: Hash maps track counts or existence in O(1) average time. They are the go-to structure for problems that ask you to find duplicates, check whether two groups have the same elements, or count frequencies.

data.title: Hash map: find the first non-repeating character
data.content: Count frequencies in a first pass, then scan for the first character with count 1.

items.text: Clarify the input and output with the interviewer.
items.hint: Ask about edge cases: empty input, duplicates, large values.

items.text: Identify the dominant operation: search, insert, iterate, or aggregate?
items.hint: This points directly to the right data structure.

items.text: Start with a brute-force solution and state its complexity.
items.hint: It shows you understand the problem even if you optimize later.

items.text: Optimize using a known pattern and explain the trade-offs.
items.hint: Mention time, space, and any assumptions you are making.

items.text: Test your code with examples and boundary cases.
items.hint: Walk through at least two examples aloud.

data.title: Pattern recognition
data.text: Most interview problems are variations of a small set of patterns. Practice naming the pattern out loud: two pointers, sliding window, BFS, DFS, hash map frequency. That habit makes complex problems feel familiar.

data.title: Key takeaways
points: Two pointers reduce nested loops on sorted arrays.
Sliding windows solve contiguous subarray problems efficiently.
BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
Hash maps track frequency and existence in O(1) average time.
data.takeaway: Pattern recognition turns unfamiliar interview questions into familiar, solvable problems.
